extracted.intended_audience: regulatory economists, agency analysts, policymakers, employers, and legal counsel participating in notice-and-comment on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Economic and regulatory-impact analysis for the FTC final rule on non-competes: formulas, parameter assumptions, and sensitivity analyses used to quantify/monetize costs, benefits, distributional effects, and break-even points over a ten-year horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Decreased Investment in Advanced Training
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect of Decreased Investment in Advanced Training = Additional Output of Workers Resulting from Less Time Spent Training + Reduced Direct Outlays on Training − Lost Output Resulting from Foregone Advanced Training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition is used to represent upper-bound costs when lost investment is assumed to be 'advanced' human capital (i.e., costly investments that raise long-term productivity). The first two components are calculated elsewhere (Part X.F.7.a.i) and the lost-output term is computed using the Lost Output formula below. The net effect subtracts lost productivity from the savings from less time spent training and reduced training outlays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Output from Lost Investment in Human Capital (formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost Output from Lost Investment in Human Capital = (Total # of Affected Workers) * (Percentage Point Decrease in Trained Workers) * (Average Hourly Output of Workers) * (Average Hours Worked per Year) * (% Productivity Loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission parameter values used as examples: Total affected workers = 101.1 million (all workers) or 45.3 million (high-use occupations only); Percentage point decrease in trained workers = 0.4; Average hourly output = $60.77; Average hours/year = 1,784; % Productivity loss = 6.4%. These inputs produce year-by-year lost-output estimates which feed into ten-year discounted totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depreciation and Ten-Year Horizon for Training Returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Returns to advanced training are assumed to persist with depreciation: returns from a given year's training depreciate by 20% each subsequent year; new rounds of forgone training occur each year through year ten; lost output in year t is the sum of depreciated returns from prior years plus lost output from that year's forgone training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate lost productivity for each prior-year training separately, sum across years, then subtract from the other two components. Ten-year discounted effects presented at discount rates of 2%, 3%, and 7%. Example outputs shown in Table 5 for core vs advanced training assumptions and for all occupations vs high-use occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal Costs: components and aggregate formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal Costs = Modify Standard Contract Language/H.R. Materials and Manuals Costs + Revise Contractual Practices Costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis identifies two main legal-cost components: (1) one-time modification of standard contract language and HR materials for incoming workers; (2) firm-level advice and revisions to contractual practices (including identifying senior executives and strategizing alternatives). These are estimated by multiplying average lawyer hours by an hourly cost and the number of affected businesses, with sensitivity analyses for outside counsel rates and hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify Standard Contract Language/H.R. Materials and Manuals (calculation and assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify Standard Contract Language/H.R. Materials and Manuals = (Average Hours Necessary for Modification) * (Cost per Hour) * (# of Affected Businesses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission assumptions: average modification = 1 hour of a lawyer's time; cost per hour = $134.62 (2023$); # affected businesses = 3.4 million; yields $457 million one-time. Sensitivity: replacing $134.62 with outside-counsel rate ($483/hr) raises this component to $1.6 billion. The Commission treats the 1-hour estimate as average across firms and notes potential heterogeneity and overlap with other legal tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise Contractual Practices Costs (calculation and assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise Contractual Practices Costs = (Average Hours Necessary to Update Contractual Practices) * (Cost per Hour) * (# of Affected Businesses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission assumptions: average firm time = 4 to 8 lawyer-hours; cost per hour = $134.62; # affected businesses = 2.9 million. Under these assumptions the one-time expenditure ranges $1.6B–$3.1B. Sensitivity using outside counsel ($483/hr) yields $5.6B–$11.3B. Commission notes exclusion of senior-executive non-competes could lower net legal costs, but it does not reduce its central estimates; heterogeneity across firms may make these numbers overestimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Costs for Notification Requirement (aggregate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice Provision Cost = Digital Notice Provision Costs + Mailed Notice Provision Costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All establishments estimated to use non-competes are assumed to engage in notification; firms may use the Commission's model notice. Total one-time notification cost estimated at $94 million (digital + mailed) under primary assumptions; alternative assumptions (e.g., lawyer-prepared notices) can raise this substantially. Time costs are measured at establishment level and not varied by number of senior executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital Notice Provision Costs (calculation and assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital Notice Provision Costs = (Average Hours Necessary to Compose and Send Notice) * (Cost per Hour) * (# of Affected Businesses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission assumption: 20 minutes (1/3 hour) by an HR specialist; cost per hour $63.70; # affected businesses 3.4 million; digital cost ≈ $72 million. Commission treats this as an average and notes firms may already have digital contact information for many workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mailed Notice Provision Costs (calculation and assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost of Mailed Notice Provision = Number of Workers with Non-competes Receiving Physical Notice * (Cost of One Printed Page + Mailing Cost + Cost of Human Resource Professional's Time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission calculation: Number receiving mail = total covered workers (101.1M) * % with non-competes (18.1%) * % requiring mailed notice (66%) = 12.3M. Per-notice cost = $0.05 (page) + $0.70 (postage) + 1 minute of HR time at $63.70/hr = $1.81; total mailed cost ≈ $22 million. Commission treats 66% as an upper-bound and flags likely overestimate since many workers receive digital communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Legal Professional Involvement in Notice (model vs attorney-drafted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission assumes model notice language is available and does not require legal professionals; it therefore excludes attorney time to draft original notice from regulatory cost estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters' alternative assuming 2 hours of legal time per notice would dramatically increase costs (Commission notes an upper-bound estimate of $5.2 billion under such assumptions). The model notice mitigates need for lawyer involvement; the Commission finds legal-professional-time assumptions for notice to be unreasonable and excludes them from primary cost totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation Effects Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative assessment: litigation related to non-competes may decrease because the rule creates bright-line rules, reducing uncertainty; conversely, litigation may increase if firms turn to trade-secret litigation or litigate over what constitutes a non-compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission finds plausible but directionally opposite theoretical outcomes across litigation types, cites some evidence that trade-secret litigation falls after non-compete bans, finds no evidence that increased litigation will raise costs materially, cannot quantify an overall litigation effect, and treats it as immaterial to the benefit–cost assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and Treatment of Transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some portion of earnings and price effects are transfers (e.g., bargaining-driven earnings increases are transfers from firms to workers; price decreases may transfer surplus from firms to consumers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When monetizing benefits, the Commission distinguishes transfers from net social benefits and notes it cannot identify what share of the earnings effect is a benefit versus a transfer without additional parameters; this distinction is central to break-even and benefit monetization analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional Effects — Firm Expansion and Formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess effects of the rule on new firm entry and incumbent firm investment: decreased enforceability may increase new firm formation but may also reduce incumbent capital investment; net economy-wide effect is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings cited: new firm formation increases by 2.7% (economy-wide) and by 3.2% in high-tech establishment entry rate. Evidence on capital investment is mixed (some studies show declines for incumbent publicly traded firms, others no effect); Commission quantifies only effects literature addresses and does not monetize unmeasured components of the tradeoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional Effects — Capital Investment (evidence interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate capital-investment impacts recognizing firm-level estimates may not translate to market-level effects because new firm entry can offset incumbent declines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites estimates such as a statistically-insignificant 7.9% decline in capital investment for average incumbent publicly traded firms, a 34%–39% decline for some high-tech samples, and a 3.1% (statistically insignificant) increase in another high-tech measure. The Commission gives more weight to granular measures and highlights uncertainty and study limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional Effects on Workers (gender, race, entrepreneurship, and legal uncertainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the rule affects wage gaps, entrepreneurship (especially for women), and legal uncertainty for relatively low-paid workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission finds evidence that a nationwide prohibition on non-competes may reduce gender and racial earnings gaps and increase entrepreneurship among women; the bright-line prohibition may mitigate legal-uncertainty costs for low-paid workers who lack access to legal services. These are treated as distributional benefits; some are quantified where possible but many are not monetized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor Mobility and Turnover Cost per Worker (formula and example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional Turnover Cost per Worker with a Non-compete = (Baseline Turnover Rate) * (% Increase in Turnover) * (Rate of Use of Non-competes in Affected Industries) * (Overall Earnings of Affected Workers) * (Cost of Turnover as % of Earnings) / (Number of Workers in Affected Industries with Non-competes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission parameter values: baseline turnover 47%; % increase in turnover = 1.0%; rate of non-compete use in affected industries = 23.9%; overall earnings of affected workers = $5.25T; cost of turnover as % of earnings = 25%; number of workers with non-competes in affected industries = 11.8M. These yield an annual estimated increase in turnover costs of $131 per worker with a non-compete. The Commission cautions this likely double-counts training costs (also counted elsewhere) and that increased labor supply may reduce many turnover components, so the net effect is not quantified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break-Even Analysis: equation and required monetization parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Break-even condition: (Net Costs Associated with Investment in Human Capital) + (Direct Compliance Costs) + (Costs of Updating Contracts) = (Earnings Increase) * (Benefit % of Earnings Increase) + (Patent Increase) * (Social Value of Patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission calculates net monetizable costs (e.g., $39.0B net cost associated with investment in human capital + $3.7B direct compliance and contract-updating costs = $42.7B at 3% discount). Commission reports discounted ten-year earnings increase ($468B) and patent-increase ranges (3,111 to 31,110 patents/year), and computes breakeven benefit-percent and social-patent-value pairs. Benchmarked social-patent-value assumptions include $94,886; $234,399; $5,865,833; $32,459,680. Commission also tests benefit % assumptions of 0%, 5%, 10%, 25%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discounting, timing, and baseline assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discount rates and timing: ten-year horizon; returns to training depreciate 20% per year; discounted results presented for 2%, 3%, and 7% rates. Legal and administrative costs are assumed to be borne in the first year and therefore are not discounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These timing assumptions affect present-value totals. The Commission also distinguishes assumptions about which workers are affected (all workers vs high-use occupations) and whether lost training is 'core' versus 'advanced' — these assumptions materially change whether the net monetizable effect is a benefit or a cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior Executive Exemption and Identification (treatment in cost estimates)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule excludes existing non-competes with senior executives; firms must identify senior executives whose existing non-competes are unaffected, but the Commission does not add a separate legal-cost component for identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission rationale: use of a compensation threshold and a duties-based definition (and automatic inclusion of CEO/president) makes identification not difficult or time-consuming; estimates of attorney time to revise contractual practices (4–8 hours) are intended to encompass such identification. The Commission notes exclusion may delay or reduce costs for some firms but does not reduce its central cost estimates to maintain consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analyses and scenario comparisons (recommended practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform sensitivity analyses across key parameters and alternative assumptions: e.g., hours of lawyer time (4 v. 8), in-house vs outside counsel hourly rates ($134.62 vs $483 or other), all workers affected vs high-use occupations only, lost training = core vs advanced, discount rates (2%,3%,7%), and assumed values for social value of patents and benefit-percentage of earnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission presents primary estimates along with multiple sensitivity runs (tables and narrative). It labels some assumptions conservative (e.g., assuming mailed notice share at 66% as an upper bound) and explains how different assumptions materially change net monetized outcomes (including breakeven results).
